title: Automatically Finding Reward Model Biases
claim: A reward model can prefer a response that a trusted judge rejects because of a superficial attribute, exposing a hidden bias.
layout: Stacked rows: prompt, two response boxes, RM and judge bands, outcomes right
description: A single worked example of a reward model failing. A user prompt about post-election military takeovers sits in a box at the top, with a small laptop-user icon. Below it are two monospaced response boxes. The left one is the original response with normal spacing. The right one is the alternative response with triple spaces between words, and the extra spaces are marked in red. Dotted arrows lead from both responses down to two horizontal bands. The blue band is the reward model, Skywork-V2-8B, and shows a score of 49 in a red circle for the original and 55 in a green circle for the alternative. The orange band is the LLM judge, Claude Sonnet 4.5, with a short reasoning quote that favors the original. Bold arrows on the right read 'Prefers Alternative response' for the RM and 'Prefers Original response' for the judge, so the disagreement is the focus.
caption: Between the original response with normal spacing, and the alternative response with extra whitespace characters between words, the RM mistakenly prefers the latter, disagreeing with the LLM judge.
abstract: Reward models are central to large language model (LLM) post-training. However, past work has shown that they can reward spurious or undesirable attributes such as length, format, hallucinations, and sycophancy. In this work, we introduce and study the research problem of automatically finding reward model biases in natural language. We offer a simple approach of using an LLM to iteratively propose and refine candidate biases. Our method can recover known biases and surface novel ones: for example, we found that Skywork-V2-8B, a leading open-weight reward model, often mistakenly favors responses with redundant spacing and responses with hallucinated content. In addition, we show evidence that evolutionary iteration outperforms flat best-of-N search, and we validate the recall of our pipeline using synthetically injected biases. We hope our work contributes to further research on improving RMs through automated interpretability methods.
